entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17571"/><title type="x-IS">INTRODUCTION</title> <div sID="gen35347" type="x-p"/> The headings (<reference osisRef="Eph.1.1">Ep 1:1</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Eph.3.1">Ep 3:1</reference>, show that this Epistle claims to be that of Paul. This claim is confirmed by the testimonies of Irenæus, [Against Heresies, 5.2,3; 1.8,5]; Clement of Alexandria, [Miscellanies, 4, P. 65, and The Instructor, 1.8]; Origen, [Against Celsus, 4,211]. It is quoted by Valentinus, A.D. 120, namely, <reference osisRef="Eph.3.14-Eph.3.18">Ep 3:14-18</reference>, as we know from Hippolytus [The Refutation of All Heresies, p. 193]. Polycarp [Epistle to the Philippians, 12], testifies to its canonicity. So Tertullian [Against Marcion, 5,17]. Ignatius [Epistle to the Ephesians, 12], which alludes to the frequent and affectionate mention made by Paul of the Christian state, privileges, and persons of the Ephesians in his Epistle.<div eID="gen35347" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen35346" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen35348" type="x-p"/> Two theories, besides the ordinary one, have been held on the question, to whom the Epistle is addressed. Grotius, after the heretic Marcion, maintains that it was addressed to the Church at Laodicea, and that it is the Epistle to which Paul refers in <reference osisRef="Col.4.16">Col 4:16</reference>. But the Epistle to the Colossians was probably written before that to the Ephesians, as appears from the parallel passages in Ephesians bearing marks of being expanded from those in Colossians; and Marcion seems to have drawn his notion, as to our Epistle, from Paul's allusion (<reference osisRef="Col.4.16">Col 4:16</reference>) to an Epistle addressed by him to the Laodiceans. Origen and Clement of Alexandria, and even Tertullian, who refers to Marcion, give no sanction to his notion. No single manuscript contains the heading, "to the saints that are at Laodicea." The very resemblance of the Epistle to the Ephesians, to that to the Colossians, is against the theory; for if the former were really the one addressed to Laodicea (<reference osisRef="Col.4.16">Col 4:16</reference>), Paul would not have deemed it necessary that the churches of Colosse and Laodicea should interchange Epistles. The greetings, moreover (<reference osisRef="Col.4.15">Col 4:15</reference>), which he sends through the Colossians to the Laodiceans, are quite incompatible with the idea that Paul wrote an Epistle to the Laodiceans at the same time, and by the same bearer, Tychicus (the bearer of our Epistle to the Ephesians, as well as of that to Colosse, <reference osisRef="Eph.6.21">Ep 6:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Col.4.7">Col 4:7</reference>); for who, under such circumstances, would not send the greetings directly in the letter to the party saluted? The letter to Laodicea was evidently written some time before that to Colosse, Archbishop Usher has advanced the second theory: That it was an encyclical letter headed, as in Manuscript B., "to the saints that are ... and to the faithful," the name of each Church being inserted in the copy sent to it; and that its being sent to Ephesus first, occasioned its being entitled, as now, the Epistle to the Ephesians. Alford makes the following objections to this theory: (1) It is at variance with the spirit of the Epistle, which is clearly addressed to one set of persons throughout, co-existing in one place, and as one body, and under the same circumstances. (2) The improbability that the apostle, who in two of his Epistles (Second Corinthians and Galatians) has so plainly specified their encyclical character, should have here omitted such specification. (3) The still greater improbability that he should have, as on this hypothesis must be assumed, written a circular Epistle to a district, of which Ephesus was the commercial capital, addressed to various churches within that district, yet from its very contents (as by the opponents' hypothesis) not admitting of application to the Church of that metropolis, in which he had spent so long a time, and to which he was so affectionately bound. (4) The inconsistency of this hypothesis with the address of the Epistle, and the universal testimony of the ancient Church. The absence of personal greetings is not an argument for either of the two theories; for similarly there are none in Galatians, Philippians, First and Second Thessalonians, First Timothy. The better he knows the parties addressed, and the more general and solemn the subject, the less he seems to give of these individual notices. Writing, as he does in this Epistle, on the constitution and prospects of Christ's universal Church, he refers the Ephesians, as to personal matters, to the bearer of the Epistle, Tychicus (<reference osisRef="Eph.6.21">Ep 6:21</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eph.6.22">22</reference>). As to the omission of "which are at Ephesus" (<reference osisRef="Eph.1.1">Ep 1:1</reference>), in Manuscript B., so "in Rome" (<reference osisRef="Rom.1.7">Ro 1:7</reference>) is omitted in some old manuscripts: it was probably done by churches among whom it was read, in order to generalize the reference of its contents, and especially where the subject of the Epistle is catholic. The words are found in the margin of Manuscript B, from a first hand; and are found in all the oldest manuscripts and versions.<div eID="gen35348" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35349" type="x-p"/> Paul's first visit to Ephesus (on the seacoast of Lydia, near the river Cayster) is related in <reference osisRef="Acts.18.19-Acts.18.21">Ac 18:19-21</reference>. The work, begun by his disputations with the Jews in his short visit, was carried on by Apollos (<reference osisRef="Acts.18.24-Acts.18.26">Ac 18:24-26</reference>), and Aquila and Priscilla (<reference osisRef="Acts.18.26">Ac 18:26</reference>). At his second visit, after his journey to Jerusalem, and thence to the east regions of Asia Minor, he remained at Ephesus "three years" (<reference osisRef="Acts.19.10">Ac 19:10</reference>, the "two years" in which verse are only part of the time, and <reference osisRef="Acts.20.31">Ac 20:31</reference>); so that the founding and rearing of this Church occupied an unusually large portion of the apostle's time and care; whence his language in this Epistle shows a warmth of feeling, and a free outpouring of thought, and a union in spiritual privileges and hope between him and them (<reference osisRef="Eph.1.3">Ep 1:3</reference>, &c.), such as are natural from one so long and so intimately associated with those whom he addresses. On his last journey to Jerusalem, he sailed by Ephesus and summoned the elders of the Ephesian Church to meet him at Miletus, where he delivered his remarkable farewell charge (<reference osisRef="Acts.20.18-Acts.20.35">Ac 20:18-35</reference>).<div eID="gen35349" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35350" type="x-p"/> This Epistle was addressed to the Ephesians during the early part of his imprisonment at Rome, immediately after that to the Colossians, to which it bears a close resemblance in many passages, the apostle having in his mind generally the same great truths in writing both. It is an undesigned proof of genuineness that the two Epistles, written about the same date, and under the same circumstances, bear a closer mutual resemblance than those written at distant dates and on different occasions. Compare <reference osisRef="Eph.1.7">Ep 1:7</reference> with <reference osisRef="Col.1.14">Col 1:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.1.10">Ep 1:10</reference> with <reference osisRef="Col.1.20">Col 1:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.3.2">Ep 3:2</reference> with <reference osisRef="Col.1.25">Col 1:25</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.5.19">Ep 5:19</reference> with <reference osisRef="Col.3.16">Col 3:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.6.22">Ep 6:22</reference> with <reference osisRef="Col.4.8">Col 4:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.1.19">Ep 1:19</reference>; 2:5 with <reference osisRef="Col.2.12">Col 2:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.13">13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.4.2-Eph.4.4">Ep 4:2-4</reference> with <reference osisRef="Col.3.12-Col.3.15">Col 3:12-15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.4.16">Ep 4:16</reference> with <reference osisRef="Col.2.19">Col 2:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.4.32">Ep 4:32</reference> with <reference osisRef="Col.3.13">Col 3:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.4.22-Eph.4.24">Ep 4:22-24</reference> with <reference osisRef="Col.3.9">Col 3:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Col.3.10">10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.5.6-Eph.5.8">Ep 5:6-8</reference> with <reference osisRef="Col.3.6-Col.3.8">Col 3:6-8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.5.15">Ep 5:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eph.5.16">16</reference> with <reference osisRef="Col.4.5">Col 4:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.6.19">Ep 6:19</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eph.6.20">20</reference> with <reference osisRef="Col.4.3">Col 4:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Col.4.4">4</reference>; Ep 5:22-33; 6:1-9 with <reference osisRef="Col.3.18">Col 3:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.4.24">Ep 4:24</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eph.4.25">25</reference> with <reference osisRef="Col.3.9">Col 3:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.5.20-Eph.5.22">Ep 5:20-22</reference> with <reference osisRef="Col.3.17">Col 3:17</reference>, <reference osisRef="Col.3.18">18</reference>. Tychicus and Onesimus were being sent to Colosse, the former bearing the two Epistles to the two churches respectively, the latter furnished with a letter of recommendation to Philemon, his former master, residing at Colosse. The date was probably about four years after his parting with the Ephesian elders at Miletus (<reference osisRef="Acts.20.6-Acts.20.38">Ac 20:6-38</reference>), about A.D. 62, before his imprisonment had become of the more severe kind, which appears in his Epistle to the Philippians. From <reference osisRef="Eph.6.19">Ep 6:19</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eph.6.20">20</reference> it is plain he had at the time, though a prisoner, some degree of freedom in preaching, which accords with <reference osisRef="Acts.28.23">Ac 28:23</reference>, 30, 31, where he is represented as receiving at his lodgings all inquirers. His imprisonment began in February A.D. 61 and lasted "two whole years" (<reference osisRef="Acts.28.30">Ac 28:30</reference>) at least, and perhaps longer.<div eID="gen35350" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35351" type="x-p"/> The Church of Ephesus was made up of converts partly from the Jews and partly from the Gentiles (<reference osisRef="Acts.19.8-Acts.19.10">Ac 19:8-10</reference>). Accordingly, the Epistle so addresses a Church constituted (<reference osisRef="Eph.2.14-Eph.2.22">Ep 2:14-22</reference>). Ephesus was famed for its idol temple of Artemis or Diana, which, after its having been burnt down by Herostratus on the night that Alexander the Great was born (355 B.C.), was rebuilt at enormous cost and was one of the wonders of the world. Hence, perhaps, have arisen his images in this Epistle drawn from a beautiful temple: the Church being in true inner beauty that which the temple of the idol tried to realize in outward show (<reference osisRef="Eph.2.19-Eph.2.22">Ep 2:19-22</reference>). The Epistle (<reference osisRef="Eph.4.17">Ep 4:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.5.1-Eph.5.13">5:1-13</reference>) implies the profligacy for which the Ephesian heathen were notorious. Many of the same expressions occur in the Epistle as in Paul's address to the Ephesian elders. Compare <reference osisRef="Eph.1.6">Ep 1:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.7">7</reference>; 2:7, as to "grace," with <reference osisRef="Acts.20.24">Ac 20:24</reference>, <reference osisRef="Acts.20.32">32</reference>: this may well be called "the Epistle of the grace of God" [Alford]. Also, as to his "bonds," <reference osisRef="Eph.3.1">Ep 3:1</reference>, and 4:1 with <reference osisRef="Acts.20.22">Ac 20:22</reference>, <reference osisRef="Acts.20.23">23</reference>. Also <reference osisRef="Eph.1.11">Ep 1:11</reference>, as to "the counsel of God," with <reference osisRef="Acts.20.27">Ac 20:27</reference>. Also <reference osisRef="Eph.1.14">Ep 1:14</reference>, as to "the redemption of the purchased possession," with <reference osisRef="Acts.20.28">Ac 20:28</reference>. Also <reference osisRef="Eph.1.14">Ep 1:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.18">18</reference>; 2:20; 5:5, as to "building up" the "inheritance," with <reference osisRef="Acts.20.32">Ac 20:32</reference>.<div eID="gen35351" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35352" type="x-p"/> The object of the Epistle is "to set forth the ground, the course, and the aim and end of THE Church of the Faithful in Christ. He speaks to the Ephesians as a type or sample of the Church universal" [Alford]. Hence, "the Church" throughout the Epistle is spoken of in the singular, not in the plural, "churches." The Church's foundation, its course, and its end, are his theme alike in the larger and smaller divisions of the whole Epistle. "Everywhere the foundation of the Church is in the will of the Father; the course of the Church is by the satisfaction of the Son; the end of the Church is the life in the Holy Spirit" [Alford]. Compare respectively <reference osisRef="Eph.1.11">Ep 1:11</reference>; 2:5; 3:16. This having been laid down as a matter of doctrine (this part closing with a sublime doxology, <reference osisRef="Eph.3.14-Eph.3.21">Ep 3:14-21</reference>), is then made the ground of practical exhortations. In these latter also (from <reference osisRef="Eph.4.1">Ep 4:1</reference>, onward), the same threefold division prevails, for the Church is represented as founded on the counsel of "God the Father, who is above all, through all, and in all," reared by the "one Lord," Jesus Christ, through the "one Spirit" (<reference osisRef="Eph.4.4-Eph.4.6">Ep 4:4-6</reference>, &c.), who give their respective graces to the several members. These last are therefore to exercise all these graces in the several relations of life, as husbands, wives, servants, children, &c. The conclusion is that we must put on "the whole armor of God" (<reference osisRef="Eph.6.13">Ep 6:13</reference>).<div eID="gen35352" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35353" type="x-p"/> The sublimity of the STYLE and LANGUAGE corresponds to the sublimity of the subjects and exceeds almost that of any part of his Epistles. It is appropriate that those to whom he so wrote were Christians long grounded in the faith. The very sublimity is the cause of the difficulty of the style, and of the presence of peculiar expressions occurring, not found elsewhere.<div eID="gen35353" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">CHAPTER 1</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Eph.1.1-Eph.1.23">Ep 1:1-23</reference>. Thanksgiving and Prayer that They May Fully Know God's Gracious Power in Christ towards the Saints.</title> <div sID="gen35354" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17571"/><hi type="bold">1. by--</hi>rather, "through the will of God": called to the apostleship through that same "will" which originated the Church (<reference osisRef="Eph.1.5">Ep 1:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.9.11">9, 11</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Gal.1.4">Ga 1:4</reference>).<div eID="gen35354" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35355" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">which are at Ephesus--</hi>(See Introduction.)<div eID="gen35355" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35356" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to the saints ... and to the faithful--</hi>The same persons are referred to by both designations, as the Greek proves: "to those who are saints, and faithful in Christ Jesus." The sanctification by God is here put before man's faith. The twofold aspect of salvation is thus presented, God's grace in the first instance sanctifying us, (that is, setting us apart in His eternal purposes as holy unto Himself); and our faith, by God's gift, laying hold of salvation (<reference osisRef="2Thess.2.13">2Th 2:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Pet.1.2">1Pe 1:2</reference>). <div eID="gen35356" type="x-p"/>

In whom--</hi>"the Beloved" (<reference osisRef="Eph.1.6">Ep 1:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.3.24">Ro 3:24</reference>).<div eID="gen35379" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35380" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">we have--</hi>as a present possession.<div eID="gen35380" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35381" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">redemption--</hi>Greek, "our (literally, 'the') redemption"; THE redemption which is the grand subject of all revelation, and especially of the New Testament (<reference osisRef="Rom.3.24">Ro 3:24</reference>), namely, from the power, guilt, and penal consequences of sin (<reference osisRef="Matt.1.21">Mt 1:21</reference>). If a man were unable to redeem himself from being a bond-servant, his kinsman might redeem him (<reference osisRef="Lev.25.48">Le 25:48</reference>). Translate, "Unto the dispensation of the fulness of the times," that is, "which He purposed in Himself" (<reference osisRef="Eph.1.9">Ep 1:9</reference>) with a view to the economy of (the gracious administration belonging to) the fulness of the times (Greek, "fit times," "seasons"). More comprehensive than "the fulness of the time" (<reference osisRef="Gal.4.4">Ga 4:4</reference>). The whole of the Gospel times (plural) is meant, with the benefits to the Church dispensed in them severally and successively. Compare "the ages to come" (<reference osisRef="Eph.2.7">Ep 2:7</reference>). "The ends of the ages" (Greek, <reference osisRef="1Cor.10.11">1Co 10:11</reference>); "the times (same Greek as here, 'the seasons,' or 'fitly appointed times') of the Gentiles" (<reference osisRef="Luke.21.24">Lu 21:24</reference>); "the seasons which the Father hath put in His own power" (<reference osisRef="Acts.1.7">Ac 1:7</reference>); "the times of restitution of all things which God hath spoken by the prophets since the world began" (<reference osisRef="Acts.3.20">Ac 3:20</reference>, <reference osisRef="Acts.3.21">21</reference>). The coming of Jesus at the first advent, "in the fulness of time," was one of these "times." The descent of the Holy Ghost, "when Pentecost was fully come" (<reference osisRef="Acts.2.1">Ac 2:1</reference>), was another. The testimony given by the apostles to Him "in due time" ("in its own seasons," Greek) (<reference osisRef="1Tim.2.6">1Ti 2:6</reference>) was another. The conversion of the Jews "when the times of the Gentiles are fulfilled," the second coming of Christ, the "restitution of all things," the millennial kingdom, the new heaven and earth, shall be severally instances of "the dispensation of the fulness of the times," that is, "the dispensation of" the Gospel events and benefits belonging to their respective "times," when severally filled up or completed. God the Father, according to His own good pleasure and purpose, is the Dispenser both of the Gospel benefits and of their several fitting times (<reference osisRef="Acts.1.7">Ac 1:7</reference>).<div eID="gen35392" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35393" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">gather together in one--</hi>Greek, "sum up under one head"; "recapitulate." The "good pleasure which He purposed," was "to sum up all things (Greek, 'THE whole range of things') in Christ (Greek, 'the Christ,' that is, His Christ)" [Alford]. God's purpose is to sum up the whole creation in Christ, the Head of angels, with whom He is linked by His invisible nature, and of men with whom He is linked by His humanity; of Jews and Gentiles; of the living and the dead (<reference osisRef="Eph.3.15">Ep 3:15</reference>); of animate and inanimate creation. Sin has disarranged the creature's relation of subordination to God. God means to gather up all together in Christ; or as <reference osisRef="Col.1.20">Col 1:20</reference> says, "By Him to reconcile all things unto Himself, whether things in earth or things in heaven." Alford well says, "The Church of which the apostle here mainly treats, is subordinated to Him in the highest degree of conscious and joyful union; those who are not His spiritually, in mere subjugation, yet consciously; the inferior tribes of creation unconsciously; but objectively, all are summed up in Him." <div eID="gen35393" type="x-p"/>

navigation_sections.content_plain: INTRODUCTION The headings ( Ep 1:1 , and Ep 3:1 , show that this Epistle claims to be that of Paul. This claim is confirmed by the testimonies of Irenæus, [Against Heresies, 5.2,3; 1.8,5]; Clement of Alexandria, [Miscellanies, 4, P. 65, and The Instructor, 1.8]; Origen, [Against Celsus, 4,211]. It is quoted by Valentinus, A.D. 120, namely, Ep 3:14-18 , as we know from Hippolytus [The Refutation of All Heresies, p. 193]. Polycarp [Epistle to the Philippians, 12], testifies to its canonicity. So Tertullian [Against Marcion, 5,17]. Ignatius [Epistle to the Ephesians, 12], which alludes to the frequent and affectionate mention made by Paul of the Christian state, privileges, and persons of the Ephesians in his Epistle. Two theories, besides the ordinary one, have been held on the question, to whom the Epistle is addressed. Grotius, after the heretic Marcion, maintains that it was addressed to the Church at Laodicea, and that it is the Epistle to which Paul refers in Col 4:16 . But the Epistle to the Colossians was probably written before that to the Ephesians, as appears from the parallel passages in Ephesians bearing marks of being expanded from those in Colossians; and Marcion seems to have drawn his notion, as to our Epistle, from Paul's allusion ( Col 4:16 ) to an Epistle addressed by him to the Laodiceans. Origen and Clement of Alexandria, and even Tertullian, who refers to Marcion, give no sanction to his notion. No single manuscript contains the heading, "to the saints that are at Laodicea." The very resemblance of the Epistle to the Ephesians, to that to the Colossians, is against the theory; for if the former were really the one addressed to Laodicea ( Col 4:16 ), Paul would not have deemed it necessary that the churches of Colosse and Laodicea should interchange Epistles. The greetings, moreover ( Col 4:15 ), which he sends through the Colossians to the Laodiceans, are quite incompatible with the idea that Paul wrote an Epistle to the Laodiceans at the same time, and by the same bearer, Tychicus (the bearer of our Epistle to the Ephesians, as well as of that to Colosse, Ep 6:21 ; Col 4:7 ); for who, under such circumstances, would not send the greetings directly in the letter to the party saluted? The letter to Laodicea was evidently written some time before that to Colosse, Archbishop Usher has advanced the second theory: That it was an encyclical letter headed, as in Manuscript B., "to the saints that are ... and to the faithful," the name of each Church being inserted in the copy sent to it; and that its being sent to Ephesus first, occasioned its being entitled, as now, the Epistle to the Ephesians. Alford makes the following objections to this theory: (1) It is at variance with the spirit of the Epistle, which is clearly addressed to one set of persons throughout, co-existing in one place, and as one body, and under the same circumstances. (2) The improbability that the apostle, who in two of his Epistles (Second Corinthians and Galatians) has so plainly specified their encyclical character, should have here omitted such specification. (3) The still greater improbability that he should have, as on this hypothesis must be assumed, written a circular Epistle to a district, of which Ephesus was the commercial capital, addressed to various churches within that district, yet from its very contents (as by the opponents' hypothesis) not admitting of application to the Church of that metropolis, in which he had spent so long a time, and to which he was so affectionately bound. (4) The inconsistency of this hypothesis with the address of the Epistle, and the universal testimony of the ancient Church. The absence of personal greetings is not an argument for either of the two theories; for similarly there are none in Galatians, Philippians, First and Second Thessalonians, First Timothy. The better he knows the parties addressed, and the more general and solemn the subject, the less he seems to give of these individual notices. Writing, as he does in this Epistle, on the constitution and prospects of Christ's universal Church, he refers the Ephesians, as to personal matters, to the bearer of the Epistle, Tychicus ( Ep 6:21 , 22 ). As to the omission of "which are at Ephesus" ( Ep 1:1 ), in Manuscript B., so "in Rome" ( Ro 1:7 ) is omitted in some old manuscripts: it was probably done by churches among whom it was read, in order to generalize the reference of its contents, and especially where the subject of the Epistle is catholic. The words are found in the margin of Manuscript B, from a first hand; and are found in all the oldest manuscripts and versions. Paul's first visit to Ephesus (on the seacoast of Lydia, near the river Cayster) is related in Ac 18:19-21 . The work, begun by his disputations with the Jews in his short visit, was carried on by Apollos ( Ac 18:24-26 ), and Aquila and Priscilla ( Ac 18:26 ). At his second visit, after his journey to Jerusalem, and thence to the east regions of Asia Minor, he remained at Ephesus "three years" ( Ac 19:10 , the "two years" in which verse are only part of the time, and Ac 20:31 ); so that the founding and rearing of this Church occupied an unusually large portion of the apostle's time and care; whence his language in this Epistle shows a warmth of feeling, and a free outpouring of thought, and a union in spiritual privileges and hope between him and them ( Ep 1:3 , &c.), such as are natural from one so long and so intimately associated with those whom he addresses. On his last journey to Jerusalem, he sailed by Ephesus and summoned the elders of the Ephesian Church to meet him at Miletus, where he delivered his remarkable farewell charge ( Ac 20:18-35 ). This Epistle was addressed to the Ephesians during the early part of his imprisonment at Rome, immediately after that to the Colossians, to which it bears a close resemblance in many passages, the apostle having in his mind generally the same great truths in writing both. It is an undesigned proof of genuineness that the two Epistles, written about the same date, and under the same circumstances, bear a closer mutual resemblance than those written at distant dates and on different occasions. Compare Ep 1:7 with Col 1:14 ; Ep 1:10 with Col 1:20 ; Ep 3:2 with Col 1:25 ; Ep 5:19 with Col 3:16 ; Ep 6:22 with Col 4:8 ; Ep 1:19 ; 2:5 with Col 2:12 , 13 ; Ep 4:2-4 with Col 3:12-15 ; Ep 4:16 with Col 2:19 ; Ep 4:32 with Col 3:13 ; Ep 4:22-24 with Col 3:9 , 10 ; Ep 5:6-8 with Col 3:6-8 ; Ep 5:15 , 16 with Col 4:5 ; Ep 6:19 , 20 with Col 4:3 , 4 ; Ep 5:22-33; 6:1-9 with Col 3:18 ; Ep 4:24 , 25 with Col 3:9 ; Ep 5:20-22 with Col 3:17 , 18 . Tychicus and Onesimus were being sent to Colosse, the former bearing the two Epistles to the two churches respectively, the latter furnished with a letter of recommendation to Philemon, his former master, residing at Colosse. The date was probably about four years after his parting with the Ephesian elders at Miletus ( Ac 20:6-38 ), about A.D. 62, before his imprisonment had become of the more severe kind, which appears in his Epistle to the Philippians. From Ep 6:19 , 20 it is plain he had at the time, though a prisoner, some degree of freedom in preaching, which accords with Ac 28:23 , 30, 31, where he is represented as receiving at his lodgings all inquirers. His imprisonment began in February A.D. 61 and lasted "two whole years" ( Ac 28:30 ) at least, and perhaps longer. The Church of Ephesus was made up of converts partly from the Jews and partly from the Gentiles ( Ac 19:8-10 ). Accordingly, the Epistle so addresses a Church constituted ( Ep 2:14-22 ). Ephesus was famed for its idol temple of Artemis or Diana, which, after its having been burnt down by Herostratus on the night that Alexander the Great was born (355 B.C.), was rebuilt at enormous cost and was one of the wonders of the world. Hence, perhaps, have arisen his images in this Epistle drawn from a beautiful temple: the Church being in true inner beauty that which the temple of the idol tried to realize in outward show ( Ep 2:19-22 ). The Epistle ( Ep 4:17 ; 5:1-13 ) implies the profligacy for which the Ephesian heathen were notorious. Many of the same expressions occur in the Epistle as in Paul's address to the Ephesian elders. Compare Ep 1:6 , 7 ; 2:7, as to "grace," with Ac 20:24 , 32 : this may well be called "the Epistle of the grace of God" [Alford]. Also, as to his "bonds," Ep 3:1 , and 4:1 with Ac 20:22 , 23 . Also Ep 1:11 , as to "the counsel of God," with Ac 20:27 . Also Ep 1:14 , as to "the redemption of the purchased possession," with Ac 20:28 . Also Ep 1:14 , 18 ; 2:20; 5:5, as to "building up" the "inheritance," with Ac 20:32 . The object of the Epistle is "to set forth the ground, the course, and the aim and end of THE Church of the Faithful in Christ. He speaks to the Ephesians as a type or sample of the Church universal" [Alford]. Hence, "the Church" throughout the Epistle is spoken of in the singular, not in the plural, "churches." The Church's foundation, its course, and its end, are his theme alike in the larger and smaller divisions of the whole Epistle. "Everywhere the foundation of the Church is in the will of the Father; the course of the Church is by the satisfaction of the Son; the end of the Church is the life in the Holy Spirit" [Alford]. Compare respectively Ep 1:11 ; 2:5; 3:16. This having been laid down as a matter of doctrine (this part closing with a sublime doxology, Ep 3:14-21 ), is then made the ground of practical exhortations. In these latter also (from Ep 4:1 , onward), the same threefold division prevails, for the Church is represented as founded on the counsel of "God the Father, who is above all, through all, and in all," reared by the "one Lord," Jesus Christ, through the "one Spirit" ( Ep 4:4-6 , &c.), who give their respective graces to the several members. These last are therefore to exercise all these graces in the several relations of life, as husbands, wives, servants, children, &c. The conclusion is that we must put on "the whole armor of God" ( Ep 6:13 ). The sublimity of the STYLE and LANGUAGE corresponds to the sublimity of the subjects and exceeds almost that of any part of his Epistles. It is appropriate that those to whom he so wrote were Christians long grounded in the faith. The very sublimity is the cause of the difficulty of the style, and of the presence of peculiar expressions occurring, not found elsewhere.
